questions.stem: The nervous system is divided into central and peripheral parts. Which structures form the central part?
options: The cranial and spinal nerves
The brain and spinal cord
The brain and cranial nerves
The spinal cord and spinal nerves
questions.explanation: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. The cranial and spinal nerves that connect it to the rest of the body form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: In which direction do afferent neurons carry impulses?
options: From receptors towards the central nervous system
From the central nervous system towards effectors
From one side of the brain to the other side
From the spinal cord upwards to the cerebellum only
questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) neurons carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Efferent (motor) neurons carry impulses away from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands.

questions.stem: Which effectors are controlled by the somatic nervous system?
options: Skeletal muscles
Cardiac muscle
Smooth muscle in the gut
Sweat and salivary glands
questions.explanation: The somatic division carries efferent impulses to skeletal muscles, which are usually under voluntary control. Cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands are controlled by the autonomic division.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the autonomic and somatic nervous systems?
options: Autonomic pathways use one motor neuron; somatic pathways use two neurons and a ganglion
Autonomic pathways are mostly voluntary; somatic pathways are always involuntary
Autonomic pathways carry sensory impulses; somatic pathways carry motor impulses
Autonomic pathways use two neurons with a ganglion between them; somatic pathways use one
questions.explanation: In the autonomic system a preganglionic neuron from the CNS synapses in a ganglion with a postganglionic neuron that reaches the effector. A somatic motor neuron runs all the way from the CNS to the skeletal muscle. The autonomic system is involuntary.

questions.stem: Which description best fits the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system?
options: It prepares the body for action when under stress
It promotes digestion and conserves energy at rest
It controls voluntary movement of the skeletal muscles
It carries sensory impulses from the skin to the brain
questions.explanation: The sympathetic division produces the fight-or-flight response, such as a faster heart rate and the release of glucose. Promoting digestion and conserving energy describes the parasympathetic division.

questions.stem: Which response is caused by parasympathetic stimulation?
options: Release of glucose by the liver
Increase in the heart rate
Constriction of the pupils
Dilation of the bronchioles
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic division constricts the pupils, slows the heart and stimulates digestion. Dilating the bronchioles, releasing glucose and speeding the heart are sympathetic effects that prepare the body for activity.

questions.stem: A person is startled by a loud bang. Which combination of changes would the sympathetic nervous system produce?
options: Slower heart rate, dilated pupils and reduced activity of the gut
Slower heart rate, constricted pupils and increased saliva secretion
Faster heart rate, dilated pupils and reduced activity of the gut
Faster heart rate, constricted pupils and increased activity of the gut
questions.explanation: The sympathetic response diverts resources to activity: the heart speeds up, pupils dilate to let in more light, and digestion slows. Constricted pupils and increased gut activity are parasympathetic effects.

questions.stem: Most organs receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves. Why is this arrangement useful?
options: The two divisions have identical effects, so one can take over if the other fails
One division carries sensory impulses while the other carries motor impulses
One division acts only during sleep and the other acts only while awake
The two divisions have opposing effects, allowing fine control of the organ
questions.explanation: The divisions usually act antagonistically: for example, sympathetic nerves speed the heart and the vagus nerve (parasympathetic) slows it. Adjusting the balance between them allows precise control. Both divisions are efferent.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the action of the parasympathetic nerves to the heart. What would most likely happen to the resting heart rate, and why?
options: It would rise, because the slowing influence of the parasympathetic nerves is removed
It would fall, because the parasympathetic nerves normally speed up the heart
It would rise, because the drug stimulates the somatic nerves to the cardiac muscle
It would not change, because the heart is controlled only by sympathetic nerves
questions.explanation: At rest, parasympathetic impulses along the vagus nerve continually slow the heart. Blocking them leaves the sympathetic influence unopposed, so the heart rate rises. The heart is not controlled by somatic nerves.

questions.stem: A neuron carries impulses from the spinal cord to the smooth muscle in the wall of the bladder. How is it best classified?
options: Peripheral, efferent and autonomic
Peripheral, afferent and autonomic
Central, efferent and somatic
Peripheral, efferent and somatic
questions.explanation: The neuron lies outside the CNS (peripheral), carries impulses away from the CNS (efferent) and supplies smooth muscle, an involuntary effector (autonomic). Somatic neurons supply skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: How many pairs of cranial nerves and spinal nerves are there in the human peripheral nervous system?
options: 31 pairs of cranial nerves and 12 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 24 pairs of spinal nerves
10 pairs of cranial nerves and 33 pairs of spinal nerves
12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
questions.explanation: Twelve pairs of cranial nerves arise from the brain and 31 pairs of spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord. Together they form the peripheral nervous system.

questions.stem: Which part of the brain is responsible for conscious thought, memory and voluntary movement?
options: Cerebrum
Cerebellum
Medulla oblongata
Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The cerebrum, the largest part of the brain, carries out conscious thought, learning, memory, interpretation of sensations and initiation of voluntary movement. The cerebellum coordinates movement but does not initiate it.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the corpus callosum?
options: Connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres
Connecting the cerebrum to the spinal cord below
Producing cerebrospinal fluid inside the brain
Controlling the release of pituitary hormones
questions.explanation: The corpus callosum is a broad band of nerve fibres (white matter) that carries impulses between the two cerebral hemispheres, allowing them to share information.

questions.stem: After drinking a lot of alcohol, a person walks unsteadily and has poorly coordinated movements. Which part of the brain is most affected?
options: Medulla oblongata
Cerebellum
Corpus callosum
Hypothalamus
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity, posture and balance, fine-tuning movements started by the cerebrum. Impaired cerebellar function produces unsteady, poorly coordinated movement.

questions.stem: Damage to the medulla oblongata is often fatal. Why?
options: It contains the centres that control breathing and heart rate
It contains the centres for conscious thought and memory
It is the only connection between the two cerebral hemispheres
It produces all of the hormones released by the pituitary
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata contains the cardiovascular and respiratory centres, which control heart rate, blood vessel diameter and breathing. It also controls reflexes such as swallowing, coughing and vomiting.

questions.stem: Which set of functions is controlled by the hypothalamus?
options: Heart rate, breathing rate, coughing and swallowing
Language, reasoning and interpretation of sensations
Body temperature, thirst, hunger and pituitary secretion
Balance, posture and the coordination of fine movement
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus regulates body temperature, water balance and thirst, and hunger, and controls the pituitary gland. Heart rate and breathing are controlled by the medulla, and balance by the cerebellum.

questions.stem: A patient has surgery that cuts the corpus callosum to stop severe seizures spreading. An object is shown only to the right hemisphere, which in this patient lacks the main language centres. What is the most likely result?
options: The patient can pick the object out by touch but cannot name it
The patient can name the object but cannot pick it out by touch
The patient cannot see the object because vision has been lost
The patient can name it because the cerebellum relays the message
questions.explanation: With the corpus callosum cut, information reaching one hemisphere cannot cross to the other. The right hemisphere recognises the object and can guide the hand to it, but the language areas cannot receive the information, so the patient cannot name it.

questions.stem: How are grey matter and white matter arranged in the spinal cord?
options: White matter forms a butterfly shape inside, surrounded by grey matter
Grey matter and white matter are mixed evenly throughout the cord
Grey matter forms the outer layer, just as it does in the cerebrum
Grey matter forms a butterfly shape inside, surrounded by white matter
questions.explanation: In the spinal cord the grey matter, made of cell bodies and interneurons, lies in the centre, and the white matter, made of myelinated axons running up and down the cord, surrounds it. In the cerebrum the arrangement is reversed, with grey matter forming the outer cortex.

questions.stem: What are the two main roles of the spinal cord?
options: Storing memories, and linking the left and right halves of the cerebrum
Secreting hormones, and controlling the pituitary through the portal vessels
Carrying impulses between the brain and the body, and coordinating spinal reflexes
Producing cerebrospinal fluid, and controlling the heart rate and breathing rate
questions.explanation: The spinal cord conducts impulses in tracts between the brain and the body, and its grey matter can coordinate reflexes without input from the brain. Heart rate and breathing are controlled by the medulla.

questions.stem: A person's spinal cord is completely severed in the lower back. Which outcome would be expected below the injury?
options: Loss of sensation and voluntary movement, though some spinal reflexes may remain
Loss of all reflexes, though sensation and voluntary movement remain normal
Normal voluntary movement, though the person can no longer feel touch or pain
Normal sensation and movement, though the heart and breathing rates fall sharply
questions.explanation: Cutting the cord stops impulses travelling between the brain and the body below the injury, so sensation and voluntary control are lost. Reflex arcs that pass through the cord below the cut can still work because they do not need the brain.

questions.stem: Which list gives the meninges in order from the skull inwards to the brain?
options: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
questions.explanation: The tough dura mater lies against the skull, the web-like arachnoid mater is in the middle, and the delicate pia mater clings to the surface of the brain. Cerebrospinal fluid circulates in the space beneath the arachnoid.

questions.stem: Which is a function of cerebrospinal fluid?
options: Cushioning the brain and spinal cord against jolts
Carrying nerve impulses between the cerebral hemispheres
Transporting hormones from the hypothalamus to the pituitary
Insulating axons so that impulses travel more quickly
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid surrounds and supports the brain and spinal cord, absorbing shocks, and it also supplies nutrients and removes wastes. Insulating axons is the role of the myelin sheath.

questions.stem: Which bones protect the spinal cord?
options: The pelvis and the sacrum alone
The vertebrae of the vertebral column
The ribs and sternum of the chest wall
The bones of the cranium and the face
questions.explanation: The spinal cord runs through the vertebral canal formed by the stacked vertebrae, which protect it while still allowing the back to bend. The cranium protects the brain.

questions.stem: In bacterial meningitis, the meninges become inflamed. A sample of cerebrospinal fluid is often taken to diagnose it. Why does testing this fluid help?
options: The fluid carries nerve impulses, so infection changes the speed of its signals
The fluid is identical to blood plasma, so any infection in the body shows up
The fluid circulates beneath the arachnoid layer, in contact with the inflamed meninges
The fluid is made by the skull bones, which are the first tissue to become infected
questions.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid fills the subarachnoid space between the meninges, so bacteria and white blood cells from the infection appear in it. It is produced in the brain's ventricles, not by bone, and it differs in composition from plasma.

questions.stem: What type of receptor detects changes in the solute concentration of the blood?
options: Osmoreceptor
Chemoreceptor
Thermoreceptor
Mechanoreceptor
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors, found in the hypothalamus, respond to changes in the osmotic concentration of the blood, which is important in water balance. Chemoreceptors respond to particular chemicals such as carbon dioxide or hydrogen ions.

questions.stem: Where are the osmoreceptors that control the release of ADH located?
options: In the hypothalamus
In the posterior pituitary
In the walls of the kidney tubules
In the carotid and aortic bodies
questions.explanation: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood solute concentration and stimulate the release of ADH and the sensation of thirst. The carotid and aortic bodies contain chemoreceptors.

questions.stem: Thermoreceptors are found in two main places in the body. Which pair is correct?
options: In the skin and in the hypothalamus
In the skin and in the cerebellum
In the kidneys and in the hypothalamus
In the lungs and in the medulla oblongata
questions.explanation: Peripheral thermoreceptors in the skin detect changes in external temperature, and central thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect changes in the temperature of the blood. Having both lets the body respond before core temperature changes much.

questions.stem: Chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries and aorta detect changes in which blood variables?
options: Carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions and oxygen
Glucose, insulin and glucagon concentrations
Sodium, potassium and water concentrations
Temperature, pressure and the blood flow rate
questions.explanation: The carotid and aortic bodies contain chemoreceptors that respond to carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions (pH) and low oxygen, and send impulses to the medulla, which adjusts breathing. Changes in blood glucose are detected by cells of the pancreas.

questions.stem: What are the receptors for pain called, and what form do they take?
options: Chemoreceptors, which are encapsulated corpuscles
Nociceptors, which are free nerve endings
Nociceptors, which are encapsulated corpuscles
Osmoreceptors, which are free nerve endings
questions.explanation: Pain receptors, or nociceptors, are free nerve endings that respond to stimuli that damage, or could damage, tissue. Many touch and pressure receptors, by contrast, are enclosed in capsules of connective tissue.

questions.stem: Fingertips have far more touch receptors per square centimetre than the skin of the back. What would you predict when two points are pressed on the skin close together?
options: They are felt as pain on the fingertip but only as light pressure on the back
They are felt as two separate points on the fingertip but as one on the back
They are felt as one point on the fingertip but as two separate points on the back
They are felt as two separate points at both sites, because the receptors are alike
questions.explanation: Where receptors are densely packed, two nearby points stimulate different receptors and are felt separately. On the back, both points may fall in the area served by one receptor, so they are felt as one.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes what sensory receptors do?
options: Each receptor responds equally to all stimuli and decides which response is needed
Receptors carry out the body's response to a stimulus, such as contracting a muscle
Receptors are found only in the special sense organs such as the eyes and ears
Each type of receptor responds best to one kind of stimulus and starts nerve impulses
questions.explanation: Receptors are specialised to detect particular stimuli, such as heat, chemicals or pressure, and convert them into nerve impulses carried by sensory neurons. Effectors, not receptors, carry out the response.

questions.stem: The symptoms of Parkinson's disease, such as tremor and slow movement, mainly result from what?
options: Infection of the meninges surrounding the brain
Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain
Loss of myelin from neurons in the spinal cord
Overproduction of insulin by the pancreatic islets
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease involves the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in a region of the midbrain, reducing dopamine in the areas that control movement. Loss of myelin occurs in other diseases, such as multiple sclerosis.

questions.stem: What is the aim of cell replacement therapy for Parkinson's disease?
options: Removing the damaged region of the brain so that healthy areas take over its role
Inserting the gene for insulin into neurons so they make more neurotransmitter
Transplanting new dopamine-producing neurons into the brain to replace those lost
Injecting dopamine into the bloodstream so that it reaches every neuron in the body
questions.explanation: Cell replacement therapy aims to grow dopamine-producing neurons, usually from stem cells, and transplant them into the brain region that has lost its dopamine supply. The new cells could then release dopamine where it is needed.

questions.stem: Stem cells are central to cell replacement therapy. What property makes them useful?
options: They cannot divide, so there is no risk of them forming a growth after transplant
They are taken only from the patient's brain, so they never cause rejection
They can divide and be directed to become specialised cell types such as neurons
They are already fully specialised neurons that only need to be placed in the brain
questions.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialised cells that can divide and, given the right signals, differentiate into specialised cells such as dopamine-producing neurons. Because they can keep dividing, uncontrolled growth after a transplant is one of the risks.

questions.stem: Why is cell replacement therapy considered more difficult for Alzheimer's disease than for Parkinson's disease?
options: Alzheimer's damages many types of neuron across large areas of the brain
Alzheimer's affects only the spinal cord, which cannot receive transplants
Alzheimer's is caused by a virus that would infect the transplanted cells
Alzheimer's results from too many neurons, so new cells would add to them
questions.explanation: In Parkinson's disease the main loss is one type of neuron in a fairly defined region, so a transplant target is clear. Alzheimer's disease involves the death of many kinds of neurons in widespread regions involved in memory and thinking, so replacing them and restoring their connections is far harder.

questions.stem: Researchers can reprogram a patient's own skin cells into stem cells and grow neurons from them for transplant. What is one advantage of this over using stem cells from human embryos?
options: The cells cannot divide again, removing any risk of forming a tumour
The cells are already dopamine neurons, so no further steps are needed
The cells come from the brain, so they fit existing neural connections
The cells match the patient, reducing the risk of immune rejection
questions.explanation: Cells derived from the patient carry the patient's own markers, so they are less likely to be rejected, and their use avoids the ethical objections to destroying embryos. Like other stem cells they can still divide, so tumour formation remains a risk to be tested.

questions.stem: Which is a key ethical issue raised by some forms of cell replacement therapy?
options: Obtaining stem cells from human embryos, which are destroyed in the process
Using recombinant bacteria that might escape and spread the disease to others
Giving patients a cure that would be passed on automatically to their children
Transplanting neurons that would change the patient's blood group permanently
questions.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are taken from early embryos, which are destroyed, and people disagree about the moral status of the embryo. Transplanted neurons are somatic cells, so any benefit would not be inherited.
